title: Docker Compose Basics
intro: Real apps are rarely one container — Compose lets you define and run multi-container setups (app + db + cache) with one file.

steps.prompt: Start everything defined in docker-compose.yml, in detached mode.
steps.fake_output:
Creating network "myapp_default"
Creating myapp_db_1 ... done
Creating myapp_web_1 ... done
steps.explanation: Compose creates a shared network automatically so services can reach each other by name (e.g. the app can just connect to host 'db').
steps.why: You could 'docker run' each container separately and wire up networking by hand, but Compose reads the relationships (depends_on, shared networks, volumes) from one file — the whole point is not having to remember and retype a growing pile of individual docker run flags.

steps.prompt: Check the status of all services.
steps.fake_output:
NAME          IMAGE      STATUS         PORTS
myapp_db_1    postgres   Up 10 seconds  5432/tcp
myapp_web_1   myapp      Up 10 seconds  0.0.0.0:8080->3000/tcp
steps.explanation: Same idea as docker ps, scoped to this compose project.
steps.why: Plain 'docker ps' would also show these containers, mixed in with anything else running on the machine — 'compose ps' filters to just this project, which matters once you have several compose projects running at once.

steps.prompt: Follow the logs of just the 'web' service.
steps.fake_output:
web_1  | Connecting to db:5432...
web_1  | Connected. Server started.
steps.explanation: Notice it connects to 'db' by service name, not an IP — that's Compose's internal DNS at work.
steps.why: 'docker compose logs -f' with no service name streams every service interleaved, which gets noisy fast — naming 'web' specifically is the same instinct as kubectl logs -l app=X when you only care about one thing.

steps.prompt: You changed the Dockerfile. Rebuild and restart everything.
steps.fake_output:
Building web
Step 1/5...
Successfully built
Recreating myapp_web_1 ... done
steps.explanation: --build forces a rebuild of any service with a 'build' key in the compose file before starting.
steps.why: Without --build, 'docker compose up' reuses whatever image already exists locally — your Dockerfile change would be silently ignored, which is a very common 'why isn't my change showing up' trap.

steps.prompt: Tear everything down, including the volumes.
steps.fake_output:
Stopping myapp_web_1 ... done
Stopping myapp_db_1 ... done
Removing myapp_web_1 ... done
Removing myapp_db_1 ... done
Removing volume myapp_dbdata
steps.explanation: -v also removes named volumes — without it, your database data would survive for next time, which is usually what you want in dev unless you're intentionally resetting.
steps.why: Plain 'docker compose down' (no -v) is the safer default for everyday stop/start — reach for -v specifically when you want a genuinely clean slate, like testing what a fresh install actually looks like.
